claim: A library of 61 soil and leaf-associated bacterial strains was used in this experiment.
source: A library of 61 soil and leaf-associated bacterial strains was used in this experiment.
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1A explicitly state the number and source of bacterial strains used.

claim: All strains are from four orders: Proteobacteria (orange), Firmicutes (blue), Bacteroidetes (purple), and Actinobacteria (green).
source: All strains are from four orders: Proteobacteria (orange), Firmicutes (blue), Bacteroidetes (purple), and Actinobacteria (green) (full list in Supplementary file 1a, Source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1A describe the phylogenetic composition of the strain library.

claim: Six of the 61 species were labeled with GFP and used as 'focal' species.
source: Also, 6 of the 61 species were labeled with GFP and used as 'focal' species whose growth was tested in the presence of the other isolates (affecting species).
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1A explicitly describe the focal species labeling approach.

claim: The focal species include Escherichia coli [EC], Ewingella americana [EA], Raoultella planticola [RP], Buttiauxella izardii [BI], Citrobacter freundii [CF], and Pantoea agglomerans [PA].
source: These strains are labeled on the phylogenetic tree (Escherichia coli [EC], Ewingella americana [EA], Raoultella planticola [RP], Buttiauxella izardii [BI], Citrobacter freundii [CF], and Pantoea agglomerans [PA].)
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1A explicitly list the focal species.

claim: Each focal species was grown in monoculture, with between 18 and 52 single affecting species.
source: Each focal species was grown in monoculture, with (between 18 and 52) single affecting species, and (between 153 and 1464) pairs of affecting species.
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1B describe the experimental design for single affecting species.

claim: Each focal species was grown with between 153 and 1464 pairs of affecting species.
source: Each focal species was grown in monoculture, with (between 18 and 52) single affecting species, and (between 153 and 1464) pairs of affecting species.
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1B describe the experimental design for pairs of affecting species.

claim: E. coli was grown with 3009 trios of affecting species.
source: Additionally, E. coli was grown with 3009 trios of affecting species.
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1B describe the experimental design for trios of affecting species.

claim: Effects of pairs and trios were predicted using three different models: additive, mean, and strongest.
source: Effects of pairs and trios were then predicted using the effects of single species and single species and pairs, respectively. Predictions were made using three different models: additive, mean, and strongest (detailed in 'Results' and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The manuscript text and Figure 1C describe the modeling approach used for predictions.

claim: Bacteria play important roles from driving biogeochemical cycles at the ecosystem level to supporting host health at the individual level.
source: In addition to naturally playing important roles from driving biogeochemical cycles at the ecosystem level (Cavicchioli et al., 2019; Arrigo, 2005; Falkowski et al., 2008) to supporting host health at the individual level (Berendsen et al., 2012; Manor et al., 2020; Gilbert et al., 2018)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting these roles of bacteria.

claim: Bacteria have been harnessed for biotechnological applications across industries such as food preservation, plant and animal health, biocontrol of pathogens, decomposition of toxic compounds, and production of valuable compounds.
source: bacteria have also been harnessed for countless biotechnological applications across industries such as food preservation (Motarjemi, 2002), plant and animal health (Berendsen et al., 2012; Júnior et al., 2021), biocontrol of pathogens (Köhl et al., 2019), as well as decomposition of toxic compounds, and production of valuable ones (Varjani et al., 2017; Ro et al., 2006; Fang and Smith, 2016; Mainka et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting these biotechnological applications.

claim: Understanding how microbial communities organize has proven difficult.
source: In natural environments, bacteria often form rich and complex communities, but understanding how these communities organize has proven difficult (Widder et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this challenge.

claim: The structure of microbial communities is determined by the interactions between the involved species.
source: The structure of microbial communities is determined by the interactions between the involved species (Konopka et al., 2015; Barbier et al., 2018; Qian and Akçay, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Much effort has been put into measuring pairwise interactions of different species from, and in, different environments.
source: In recent years, much effort has been put into measuring pairwise interactions of different species from, and in, different environments (Foster and Bell, 2012; Vetsigian et al., 2011; Kehe et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this research effort.

claim: It is unclear to what extent the joint effects of multiple species on a focal species can be inferred from pairwise measurements.
source: But it is still unclear to what extent the joint effects of multiple species on a focal species of interest (e.g., a pathogen) can be inferred from pairwise measurements.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this knowledge gap.

claim: Inference of joint effects from pairwise measurements may be challenging due to the presence of indirect interactions.
source: Such inference may be challenging due to the presence of indirect interactions: the affecting species may alter each other's abundances (termed interaction chains) or may modify each other's effect on the focal species (termed interaction modification, or higher-order interactions) (Sanchez, 2019; Wootton, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites references explaining the theoretical challenges.

claim: Empirical studies in recent years have shown conflicting results regarding the importance of higher order interactions and indirect effects.
source: Despite a strong theoretical foundation, empirical studies in recent years have shown conflicting results regarding the importance of higher order interactions and indirect effects (Levine et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this observation.

claim: Clear evidence of higher-order interactions has been found for some functions, such as degradation of complex molecules and antibiotic production.
source: For some functions, such as degradation of complex molecules (Sanchez-Gorostiaga et al., 2019; Gralka et al., 2020) and antibiotic production (Tyc et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2021; Westhoff et al., 2021), clear evidence of such interactions has been found.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: The presence or absence of an additional species has been shown to affect interactions and the outcome of invasion and coexistence in some systems.
source: Furthermore, in both empirical and theoretical studies, the presence or absence of an additional species has been shown to affect interactions, and even the outcome of invasion and coexistence in some systems (Mickalide and Kuehn, 2019; Chang et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Commonly used ecological models (i.e., generalized Lotka-Voltera) do not properly capture microbial community interactions, partially due to the nature of these interactions.
source: Additional theoretical work has shown that commonly used ecological models (i.e., generalized Lotka-Voltera) do not properly capture microbial community interactions, partially due to the nature of these interactions (chemically mediated as opposed to predator-prey) (Momeni et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this theoretical limitation.

claim: Other studies have shown that both structures of, and interactions within, larger communities can be accurately predicted from pairwise interactions alone using variations of ecological models.
source: However, other studies have shown that both structures of, and interactions within, larger communities can be accurately predicted from pairwise interactions alone using variations of said models (Friedman et al., 2017; Meroz et al., 2021; Guo and Boedicker, 2016; Venturelli et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: How microbial interactions combine into the joint effect of multiple species on a single species of interest is still poorly understood.
source: This being the case, how microbial interactions combine into the joint effect of multiple species on a single species of interest is still poorly understood.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this knowledge gap.

claim: High-throughput nanodroplet-based microfluidics was used to measure over 14,000 bacterial communities.
source: In our research, we used high-throughput nanodroplet-based microfluidics to measure over 14,000 bacterial communities composed of subsets of a library of 61 soil and leaf isolates of which six were fluorescently labeled (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method and scale.

claim: The effects of multiple species are dominated by the strongest single-species effect.
source: We quantified the effect of individual species and the joint effects of species pairs and trios on the growth of six focal bacterial species and found that the effects of multiple species are dominated by the strongest single-species effect, and specifically that negative effects combine non-additively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this main finding.

claim: Negative effects combine non-additively.
source: We quantified the effect of individual species and the joint effects of species pairs and trios on the growth of six focal bacterial species and found that the effects of multiple species are dominated by the strongest single-species effect, and specifically that negative effects combine non-additively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this main finding.

claim: The 61 affecting species included soil and leaf isolates as well as lab strains representing 19 genera from four phyla.
source: The 61 affecting species included soil and leaf isolates as well as lab strains representing 19 genera from four phyla: Proteobacteria (n = 14), Firmicutes (n = 2), Bacteroidetes (n = 2), and Actinobacteria (n = 1) (full list in Supplementary file 1, Source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of the strain library.

claim: The focal species were a subset of six species that were transformed to constitutively express a fluorescent protein.
source: The focal species were a subset of six of these species (all proteobacteria) that were transformed to constitutively express a fluorescent protein: (Escherichia coli [EC], Ewingella americana [EA], Raoultella planticola [RP], Buttiauxella izardii [BI], Citrobacter freundii [CF], and Pantoea agglomerans [PA]) (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The manuscript describes the focal species and their labeling.

claim: Except for EC, which is a lab strain (E. coli K-12 substr. MG1655), all focals were isolated from soil samples.
source: Except for EC, which is a lab strain (E. coli K-12 substr. MG1655), all focals were isolated from soil samples (Kehe et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the origin of the focal species.

claim: Each species was characterized phylogenetically by performing Sanger sequencing of their 16S ribosomal RNA gene.
source: First, we characterized each species phylogenetically by performing Sanger sequencing of their 16S ribosomal RNA gene and phenotypically by growing each species on each of 20 different carbon sources and 11 antibiotics.
evidence: The manuscript describes the phylogenetic characterization method.

claim: Each species was characterized phenotypically by growing each species on each of 20 different carbon sources and 11 antibiotics.
source: First, we characterized each species phylogenetically by performing Sanger sequencing of their 16S ribosomal RNA gene and phenotypically by growing each species on each of 20 different carbon sources and 11 antibiotics.
evidence: The manuscript describes the phenotypic characterization method.

claim: The species showed large variability in carbon utilization profiles with no species growing well on all carbon sources.
source: The species showed large variability in carbon utilization profiles with no species growing well on all carbon sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the carbon utilization results.

claim: There was high variability in growth on antibiotics with 15 species showing little or no growth on any antibiotics, while 16 species showed resistance to at least seven antibiotics.
source: There was also high variability in growth on antibiotics with 15 species showing little or no growth on any antibiotics, while 16 species showed resistance to at least seven antibiotics (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the antibiotic resistance results.

claim: The interaction assays were performed in the kChip microfluidics device.
source: We performed the interaction assays in the kChip microfluidics device (Kulesa et al., 2018; Kehe et al., 2019), allowing for extensive screening in parallel (see 'Materials and methods,' Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental platform used.

claim: The effects of 243 single species were measured (18–52 for each of the six focal species).
source: We measured the effects of 243 single species (18–52 for each of the six focal species), the joint effects of 5357 species pairs (between 153 and 1464 for each of the six focal species), and the joint effects of 3009 species trios (from a subset of 26 affecting species on one focal species).
evidence: The manuscript describes the number of single-species effects measured.

claim: The joint effects of 5357 species pairs were measured (between 153 and 1464 for each of the six focal species).
source: We measured the effects of 243 single species (18–52 for each of the six focal species), the joint effects of 5357 species pairs (between 153 and 1464 for each of the six focal species), and the joint effects of 3009 species trios (from a subset of 26 affecting species on one focal species).
evidence: The manuscript describes the number of pair effects measured.

claim: The joint effects of 3009 species trios were measured (from a subset of 26 affecting species on one focal species).
source: We measured the effects of 243 single species (18–52 for each of the six focal species), the joint effects of 5357 species pairs (between 153 and 1464 for each of the six focal species), and the joint effects of 3009 species trios (from a subset of 26 affecting species on one focal species).
evidence: The manuscript describes the number of trio effects measured.

claim: Cultures were normalized and mixed after pre-growth, such that the starting densities in the kChip were approximately 1:1 for all species in wells containing two droplets and two affecting species.
source: Cultures were normalized and mixed after pre-growth, such that the starting densities in the kChip were approximately 1:1 for all species in wells containing two droplets and two affecting species, but ratios varied in three droplet wells (see 'Materials and methods,' Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental setup for initial densities.

claim: Interaction assays were carried out in minimal M9 media with 0.5% [w/v] glucose for 24 hr.
source: Interaction assays were carried out in minimal M9 media with 0.5% [w/v] glucose for 24 hr.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental conditions.

claim: The growth of the focal species was measured by fluorescence.
source: The growth of the focal species was measured by fluorescence, and effects were calculated as the log ratio of growth in coculture to growth in monoculture (see 'Materials and methods,' Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the measurement method.

claim: Effects were calculated as the log ratio of growth in coculture to growth in monoculture.
source: The growth of the focal species was measured by fluorescence, and effects were calculated as the log ratio of growth in coculture to growth in monoculture (see 'Materials and methods,' Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the calculation method for effects.

claim: Positive and negative effects are defined as a net increase or decrease in growth compared to the monoculture respectively.
source: Positive and negative effects are defined as a net increase or decrease in growth compared to the monoculture respectively, while affecting species with no observable effect (see 'Materials and methods') were defined as neutral.
evidence: The manuscript defines the terminology for effect types.

claim: Individual effects covered a wide range (median = −0.15, interquartile range = 0.94).
source: Individual effects covered a wide range (median = −0.15, interquartile range = 0.94) (Figure 2A)
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the distribution of individual effects.

claim: Positive effects were common overall (32.9%).
source: and positive effects (the focal species reaching a higher density in the presence of an affecting species than in monoculture) were common overall (32.9%, Figure 2B), in line with previous studies (Kehe et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the prevalence of positive effects.

claim: The distribution of effects varied based on the focal species, with E. coli and B. izardii showing the most negative (–2.83) and positive (+0.43) median effects, respectively.
source: The distribution of effects varied based on the focal species, with E. coli and B. izardii showing the most negative (–2.83) and positive (+0.43) median effects, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the variation in effects across focal species.

claim: No affecting species had strong effects across all focal species.
source: Additionally, we found no affecting species that had strong effects across all focal species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the specificity of effects.

claim: The measured traits of individual species showed no consistent correlations with their effects on the focal species.
source: The measured traits of individual species showed no consistent correlations with their effects on the focal species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: The similarity of metabolic profile, resistance profile, or phylogeny between the focal and affecting species did not correlate strongly with the effect across focal species.
source: In particular, the similarity of metabolic profile, resistance profile, or phylogeny between the focal and affecting species did not correlate strongly with the effect across focal species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding.

claim: Most correlations between traits and effects were not statistically significant.
source: Most of these correlations were not statistically significant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the statistical significance of correlations.

claim: Negative effects were significantly more prevalent in joint pair effects (77.1%) than in effects of individual species (60.5%) (p=1.3e-9, Fisher's exact test).
source: Overall, negative effects were significantly more prevalent in joint pair effects (77.1%) than in effects of individual species (60.5%) (p=1.3e-9, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the statistical comparison of negative effects.

claim: The median effect on each focal was more negative by 0.28 on average for pairs compared to single species.
source: The median effect on each focal was more negative by 0.28 on average, though the difference was not significant in all cases; additionally, focals with mostly positive single-species interactions showed a small increase in median effect (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the change in median effects.

claim: The minimum and maximum effects for each focal species remained similar between single species and pairs.
source: Despite this, the minimum and maximum effects for each focal species remained similar.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: Pairs' joint effects did not correlate well with species traits, with similarity between the two affecting species, or with their similarity to the focal species.
source: As with the single affecting species, pairs' joint effects did not correlate well with species traits, with similarity between the two affecting species, or with their similarity to the focal species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the lack of correlation for pair effects.

claim: It may be challenging to connect the effects of single and pairs of species on a focal strain to a specific trait of the involved strains using simple analysis.
source: These results indicate that it may be challenging to connect the effects of single and pairs of species on a focal strain to a specific trait of the involved strains using simple analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: The strongest effect model best agrees with the measured effects across all species and interaction types.
source: When measured across all species and interaction types, we found that the model that best agrees with the measured effects is the strongest effect model (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the model comparison results.

claim: The strongest effect model was the most accurate overall (nRMSE = 0.46, 0.32, and 0.16 for the additive, mean, and strongest models, correspondingly).
source: The strongest effect model was the most accurate overall (nRMSE = 0.46, 0.32, and 0.16 for the additive, mean, and strongest models, correspondingly)
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative accuracy metrics for the models.

claim: The strongest effect model was considerably more accurate when both species affected the focal negatively (nRMSE = 0.65, 0.25, and 0.16).
source: and considerably more accurate when both species affected the focal negatively (nRMSE = 0.65, 0.25, and 0.16).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative accuracy metrics for negative-negative interactions.

claim: The additive model was slightly more accurate when one effect was negative and the other positive (nRMSE = 0.14, 0.43, and 0.16).
source: The additive model was slightly more accurate when one effect was negative and the other positive (nRMSE = 0.14, 0.43, and 0.16).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative accuracy metrics for mixed interactions.

claim: Predictions when both effects were positive were less accurate, but the strongest model gave the most accurate predictions (nRMSE = 0.81, 0.78, and 0.69).
source: Overall, predictions when both effects were positive were less accurate, but here too the strongest model gave the most accurate predictions (nRMSE = 0.81, 0.78, and 0.69) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure provide quantitative accuracy metrics for positive-positive interactions.

claim: When both single-species effects were negative, the mean model was prone to underestimating the combined effect.
source: The distribution of errors further supported the strongest effect model (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B): When both single-species effects were negative, the mean model was prone to underestimating the combined effect due to the reduction of the stronger effect by taking into account the weaker effect
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the error patterns for the mean model.

claim: When both single-species effects were negative, the additive model overestimated effects due to the addition of the weaker effect to the stronger effect.
source: while contrastingly, the additive model overestimated effects due to the addition of the weaker effect to the stronger effect, which was more accurate on its own.
evidence: The manuscript describes the error patterns for the additive model.

claim: When effects are close to equal, the mean model is fairly accurate while the additive model does particularly poorly.
source: When effects are close to equal, the mean model is fairly accurate while the additive model does particularly poorly as these effects would be calculated as twice the strongest effect.
evidence: The manuscript describes how effect size differences influence model accuracy.

claim: When one effect is much stronger than the other, the additive model is accurate since the addition of the weak effect is negligible.
source: Contrastly, when one effect is much stronger than the other, the additive model is accurate since the addition of the weak effect is negligible, whereas the mean model underestimates the joint effects by taking into account the weaker effect.
evidence: The manuscript describes how effect size differences influence model accuracy.

claim: Effects were stronger (more negative) in trios than in pairs.
source: Similar to what was observed in the move from single species to pairs, effects were stronger (in this case more negative effects) in trios than in the pairs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the comparison of trio and pair effects.

claim: The strongest effect model was more accurate than the additive and mean models for trios (nRMSE = 2.65, 1.23, and 0.63 for the additive, mean, and strongest models, correspondingly).
source: Additionally, as with joint pairs' effects, the strongest effect model was more accurate than the additive and mean models (nRMSE = 2.65, 1.23, and 0.63 for the additive, mean, and strongest models, correspondingly)
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative accuracy metrics for trio predictions.

claim: Similar distributions of error were seen in trios as in pairs, but further exaggerated with more extreme under and overestimation of the combined trios' effects by the mean and additive models, respectively.
source: Similar distributions of error were seen as in the pairs' effects, but further exaggerated with the more extreme under and overestimation of the combined trios' effects by the mean and additive models, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the error patterns for trio predictions.

claim: The move to pairs-based predictions improved the accuracy for both the mean and strongest model.
source: The move to pairs-based predictions improved the accuracy for both the mean and strongest model, while further pushing the additive predictions away from the observed effects (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the improvement in predictions using pair data.

claim: Even in the presence of additional species the strongest single-species effect still dominates the combined effect of a community.
source: These data suggest that even in the presence of additional species the strongest single-species effect still dominates the combined effect of a community.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the trio results.

claim: The strongest effect model is in stark contrast to models often used in antibiotic compound combinations, where additivity is often the default model.
source: This is in stark contrast to models often used in antibiotic compound combinations, despite most effects being negative, where additivity is often the default model (Bollenbach, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference and compares the findings to antibiotic combination studies.

claim: The additive model performed well for mixed effects (i.e., one negative and one positive), but only slightly better than the strongest model.
source: The additive model performed well for mixed effects (i.e., one negative and one positive), but only slightly better than the strongest model, and poorly when both species had effects of the same sign.
evidence: The manuscript describes the performance of the additive model for different interaction types.

claim: The additive model's accuracy for mixed effects may indicate that negative and positive effects act independently.
source: The additive model's accuracy for mixed effects may indicate that negative and positive effects act independently.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this interpretation of the additive model's performance.

claim: The mechanistic basis underlying the joint effects of multiple species is still unclear.
source: The mechanistic basis underlying the joint effects of multiple species is still unclear.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this knowledge gap.

claim: The affecting species' growth rate did not correlate well with their effect on some focal species.
source: However, this explanation is not consistent with the fact that the affecting species' growth rate did not correlate well with their effect on some focal species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the lack of correlation between growth rate and effect.

claim: Almost no single species or pairs had a strong effect across all focals.
source: but this does not coincide with the fact that we observed almost no single species or pairs with a strong effect across all focals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript text and figure describe the specificity of strong effects.

claim: The abundance of all species in each community was not measured (only the focal).
source: As we did not measure the abundance of all species in each community (only the focal), we cannot disentangle interaction modification (changes in per capita effect of specific species), from interaction chains (affecting the amount of an affecting species, and as such its effect on the focal)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this limitation.

claim: Further work is needed to pinpoint the exact mechanism(s) leading to the dominance of the strongest model for negative effects.
source: and further work is needed in order to pinpoint the exact mechanism(s) leading to the dominance of the strongest model for negative effects in our system.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this need for future research.

claim: It is possible that the manner in which effects combine is affected by the mechanism of interaction.
source: We also note that it is possible that the manner in which effects combine is affected by the mechanism of interaction
evidence: The manuscript proposes this possibility.

claim: Previous studies have shown that interference competition can combine additively, or even synergistically.
source: For instance, previous studies have shown that interference competition can combine additively, or even synergistically, results not seen in our work (Tyc et al., 2014; Westhoff et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing different combination patterns for interference competition.

claim: When we want to affect a single focal species in a given environment, introducing the species with the strongest effect on the focal would be sufficient to obtain the desired effect, as synergies were rare in the dataset.
source: Our results suggest that when we want to affect a single focal species in a given environment (e.g., for biocontrol of a pathogen), introducing the species with the strongest effect on the focal would be sufficient to obtain the desired effect, as synergies were rare in our dataset.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this practical implication.

claim: In cases where there are multiple strains of interest, introducing multiple species may be beneficial since different affecting species typically have strong effects on different focals.
source: In cases where there are multiple strains of interest (e.g., probiotics), introducing multiple species may be beneficial since different affecting species typically have strong effects on different focals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this practical implication.

claim: Introducing combinations of species may allow for a more robust function as the chances that one member of the community will have a strong effect on a resident species of interest is more likely.
source: Introducing combinations of species may allow for a more robust function as the chances that one member of the community will have a strong effect on a resident species of interest is more likely.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this practical implication.

claim: Further work is needed to see to what extent the findings continue to hold up in more diverse communities, other taxonomic groups, and more complex environments.
source: Further work is needed in order to deepen our understanding of how multiple species affect each other and to see to what extent our findings continue to hold up in more diverse communities, other taxonomic groups, and more complex environments.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this need for future research.

claim: Nearly all of the effects in the four member communities were negative.
source: Additionally, nearly all of the effects in the four member communities were negative, and it is unclear how mixed and positive effect modeling is affected by higher diversity.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation about four-member communities.

claim: The focal species are all from the same order (Enterobacterales), which may limit the purview of the findings.
source: Lastly, it is important to note that our focal species are all from the same order (Enterobacterales), which may also limit the purview of our findings.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this limitation.

claim: Community effects can be predicted from the strongest effect of a single species, greatly reducing the amount of information required to obtain accurate estimations.
source: Nonetheless, our results suggest that community effects can be predicted from the strongest effect of a single species, greatly reducing the amount of information required to obtain accurate estimations, which can improve our ability to use a bottom-up approach for biotechnological applications, as well as answering fundamental ecology questions.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this main conclusion.

claim: Soil and leaf samples were collected from various locations in the Faculty of Agriculture in Rehovot, Israel, on multiple dates.
source: Soil (50 ml of soil, taken from a depth of ~30 cm) and leaf samples (multiple leaves from a single plant combined into a sterile 50 ml tube) were collected from various locations in the Faculty of Agriculture in Rehovot, Israel, on multiple dates (See Source data 1 file for more information).
evidence: The manuscript describes the sample collection procedure.

claim: Each sample was diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) directly after collection and vortexed for 5 min.
source: Each sample was diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) directly after collection (1 g of soil or one leaf in 10 ml of PBS) and vortexed for 5 min.
evidence: The manuscript describes the sample processing procedure.

claim: Isolates were selected on the basis of multiple criteria: growth of transferred colony in NB liquid medium (30°C), frozen glycerol stock revival in NB (OD600 > 0.1) (30°C), and subsequent growth on M9 minimal media + 1% (w/v) glucose (OD600 > 0.1) (30°C).
source: Strains were selected on the basis of multiple criteria: growth of transferred colony in NB liquid medium (30°C), frozen glycerol stock revival in NB (OD600 > 0.1) (30°C), and subsequent growth on M9 minimal media + 1% (w/v) glucose (OD600 > 0.1) (30°C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the strain selection criteria.

claim: The full 16S gene sequences (~1500 base pairs) were obtained via Sanger sequencing and classified with a combination of RDP Classifier and BLAST.
source: The full 16S gene sequences (~1500 base pairs) were obtained via Sanger sequencing and classified with a combination of RDP Classifier (Cole et al., 2014) and BLAST (Altschul et al., 1990) (list of strains in Supplementary file 1, full phylogenetic data in Source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the sequencing and classification methods.

claim: Phylogenetic distance was calculated in Geneious Prime software using MUSCLE alignment and the UPGMA method with a HKY genetic distance model.
source: Phylogenetic distance was calculated in Geneious Prime software (version 2022.2.1, Biomatters Ltd). Sequences were aligned using MUSCLE alignment. Phylogenetic tree was built using the UPGMA method with no outgroup and a HKY genetic distance model.
evidence: The manuscript describes the phylogenetic analysis methods.

claim: Focal species were transformed with commercially available plasmid pMRE132 containing GFP2.
source: Focal species were transformed with commercially available plasmid pMRE132 containing GFP2 by Kehe et al., 2021.
evidence: The manuscript describes the transformation method and cites the source.

claim: All communities with less than three replicates were not used in the analysis.
source: All communities with less than three replicates were not used in the analysis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the data filtering criteria.

claim: Isolates were only used with focals whose monocultures were at least five times larger than the isolates autofluorescence signal, allowing to measure effects of at least –1.5.
